    Nonlinear saccade-amplitude TRF on free-viewing EEG¶

    One participant of a hybrid visual search experiment: 64-channel EEG recorded while the eyes move freely over a search display, with every fixation and saccade time-locked from the co-registered eye tracker.

    Under free viewing, fixation- and saccade-related responses follow each other every few hundred milliseconds and overlap continuously, so a single jointly fitted model deconvolves all of them at once. Four predictors are unit impulses; the fifth enters nonlinearly, as a spline expansion of saccade amplitude:

    Feature Impulse at Enters as
    fixation every fixation onset unit impulse
    ontarget fixations landing on a target unit impulse
    correct fixations and saccades of correctly answered trials unit impulse
    saccade every saccade onset unit impulse
    sacc_amp every saccade onset spl(sac_amplitude): 4 B-spline columns

    In the formula notation of event-based toolboxes such as unfold:

    fixations:  y ~ fixation + ontarget + correct
saccades:   y ~ saccade + spl(sacc_amp)

    The fixation-locked kernels span −200 to 600 ms. The two saccade blocks, saccade and sacc_amp, use a shorter −200 to 400 ms window, and they must match each other because section 6 adds them together.

    Steps¶

    1. Load the recording and build the five predictors.
    2. Scope the spline basis to the saccades, so spl() means what it does in unfold.
    3. Fit one ridge TRF, with λ chosen on R² over five cross-validation folds.
    4. Plot the kernels of the four impulse predictors.
    5. Rebuild the saccade response at chosen amplitudes from the spline kernels.

    Data¶

    Not shared. One pickle per participant under DATA_PATH:

    <subject>_eeg_data.pkl   dict with
    eeg_data     (64, n_samples) float, volts, 250 Hz, BioSemi-64 channel order
    winrej       (n_windows, 2) [start, end) sample ranges rejected as artefact
    event_data   pandas DataFrame, one row per eye-tracker/trigger event

    The notebook is committed with its outputs so it can be read without them. Needs pip install -e ".[mne]".

    1. Configuration¶

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    DATA_PATH = Path("/media/dac/Nuevo vol/EEGDATA/250_eeg_dataset")
SUBJECT = "629959"

SAMPLE_RATE = 250           # Hz, the rate the pickles ship at
WINDOW = (-0.2, 0.6)        # default delay window (fixation, ontarget, correct), seconds

# The saccade onset and its amplitude splines get a shorter window of their own.
# Keep the two identical: section 6 sums their kernels lag by lag.
SACCADE_WINDOW = (-0.2, 0.4)
FEATURE_WINDOWS = {"saccade": SACCADE_WINDOW, "sacc_amp": SACCADE_WINDOW}

# Fitted 20 ms wider on each side and trimmed, so ridge edge-ringing lands on
# the margin instead of on the kernel.
DELAY_MARGIN = 0.02

# Columns the saccade-amplitude spline puts in the design, after the drop.
N_SPLINES = 4

FEATURES = ["fixation", "ontarget", "correct", "saccade", "sacc_amp"]

# One unit of an impulse is one event, so the kernel figures read in µV per event.
# sacc_amp is left out: its sub-features are spline columns, not degrees.
FEATURE_UNITS = {name: "event" for name in ["fixation", "ontarget", "correct", "saccade"]}

# Half-decade steps from 1e-6, two decades below where the metric stops changing:
# seeing the flat bottom is what tells a plateau from a search cut short (section 4).
REGULARIZATION_GRID = np.logspace(-6, 4, 21)
N_FOLDS = 5

    2. Loading¶

    The pickle is turned into an MNE Raw carrying the standard biosemi64 montage, so kernels export as Evoked and draw as topomaps. The artefact windows in winrej become BAD_ annotations, which TRFlearn drops from every fold — no manual masking.

    Only visual-search events are used. Trials are not filtered to correct responses: correct can only carry information while incorrect trials remain in the data. With them removed it would equal fixation + saccade exactly, a linear dependency that leaves the design singular.

    Each predictor is a column over the whole recording, zero everywhere except at its events' samples. For sacc_amp the value there is the saccade's amplitude in degrees rather than 1.

    In [3]:

    Copied! 
    def load_subject(subject: str) -> tuple[mne.io.RawArray, dict]:
    """The EEG as an annotated `Raw`, and the five predictor columns."""
    path = DATA_PATH / f"{subject}_eeg_data.pkl"
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"{path} not found. The data are not shared with this repository; "
            "point DATA_PATH at a local copy, or read the committed outputs.")
    with open(path, "rb") as handle:
        recording = __import__("pickle").load(handle)

    eeg, winrej, events = (recording[key] for key in ("eeg_data", "winrej", "event_data"))
    n_samples = eeg.shape[1]

    montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("biosemi64")
    info = mne.create_info(montage.ch_names, SAMPLE_RATE, ch_types="eeg")
    raw = mne.io.RawArray(eeg, info).set_montage(montage)
    raw.set_annotations(mne.Annotations(
        onset=winrej[:, 0] / SAMPLE_RATE,
        duration=(winrej[:, 1] - winrej[:, 0]) / SAMPLE_RATE,
        description="BAD_winrej"))

    events = events[events["type"].isin(["fixation", "saccade"])
                    & (events["phase"] == "vs")]
    fixations = events[events["type"] == "fixation"]
    saccades = events[events["type"] == "saccade"]

    def train(rows, values=None):
        column = np.zeros((n_samples, 1))
        column[rows["latency"].to_numpy().astype(int), 0] = (
            1.0 if values is None else values)
        return column

    features = {
        "fixation": train(fixations),
        "ontarget": train(fixations[fixations["ontarget"] == True]),
        "correct": train(events[events["correct"] == True]),
        "saccade": train(saccades),
        "sacc_amp": train(saccades, saccades["sac_amplitude"].to_numpy()),
    }
    return raw, features

    3. Splines scoped to the saccades¶

    feature_bases attaches a basis expansion to a feature, and spline_basis is the B-spline one. Used directly, though, it would expand every sample, and a B-spline evaluated at 0 is not 0: each of the ~690 000 samples with no saccade would read as a saccade of amplitude 0. The quantile knots would also be placed on those zeros rather than on the amplitudes.

    What spl(sacc_amp) means in unfold is narrower: evaluate the basis at the amplitude where a saccade occurred, and leave zero everywhere else. spline_basis(scope="event") does exactly that:

    • fit places the knots on the saccade amplitudes only;
    • transform expands the event samples and keeps the rest at zero.

    Because the model has no intercept, the unexpanded saccade impulse is the one that carries the mean response. The splines only add how the response departs from it as amplitude changes. That split needs a column drop, which under scope="event" has to be asked for (drop="mean"): the default there is no drop, since without an onset regressor removing a column would lose the mean response. At the events a full basis sums to 1, so it would reproduce the saccade column exactly, and the design would be singular.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    # Kept in a name of its own: the fitted basis is needed again in section 6.
sacc_amp_basis = spline_basis(N_SPLINES, scope="event", drop="mean")
    # Kept in a name of its own: the fitted basis is needed again in section 6. sacc_amp_basis = spline_basis(N_SPLINES, scope="event", drop="mean")

    4. Fit¶

    One subject, so a single TRFModel rather than a TRFGroup, under cv="pooled", the default paradigm. The five folds are contiguous, non-shuffled blocks, as autocorrelated time series require. gridsearchCV scores every λ on an inner split of each training fold and keeps the one with the best mean over folds. It then refits every fold at that λ and scores it on the fold it held out, which took no part in the choice.

    λ is chosen on R², the library's default. Ridge shrinks the kernels, and R² charges for the amplitude that costs, which Pearson's r, being scale-invariant, does not see. r is what the literature reports, so extra_metrics scores it on the same held-out samples, beside R² but never choosing.

    feature_units (section 1) names what one unit of each impulse is, so the figures of section 5 read in µV per event.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    data = TRFData(features=features, y=raw, sample_rate=SAMPLE_RATE)
data.create_partitions(n_folds=N_FOLDS)

model = TRFModel(
    data, FEATURES, WINDOW,
    feature_windows=FEATURE_WINDOWS,
    feature_bases={"sacc_amp": sacc_amp_basis},
    feature_units=FEATURE_UNITS,
    cv="pooled",
    delay_margin=DELAY_MARGIN,
    feature_preprocess="Standardize",
    target_preprocess="Standardize",
)
regularization, _ = model.gridsearchCV(
    REGULARIZATION_GRID,
    metric="r2",                  # chooses λ; the default
    extra_metrics=["Pearson"],    # scored beside it, never choosing
    validation_plot=False,
)

r2 = model.metric_.cpu().numpy().ravel()
r = model.extra_metrics_["Pearson"].cpu().numpy().ravel()
print(f"λ = {regularization:.3g} | held-out R² mean {r2.mean():.4f} | "
      f"r mean {r.mean():.3f}, max {r.max():.3f} ({raw.ch_names[r.argmax()]})")
print({spec: tuple(kernel.shape) for spec, kernel in model.coef_.items()},
      "<- (channels, columns, delays)")

{'fixation': (64, 1, 201), 'ontarget': (64, 1, 201), 'correct': (64, 1, 201), 'saccade': (64, 1, 151), 'sacc_amp': (64, 4, 151)} <- (channels, columns, delays)
    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    model.validation_plot(["r2", "Pearson"], show=True);
    model.validation_plot(["r2", "Pearson"], show=True);

    Both curves are flat over the bottom of the grid. Between 1e-6 and 1e-4 the R² of the inner splits moves in its sixth decimal; it starts to fall near λ = 1e-2 and reaches zero by 1e4, where the kernels have been shrunk to nothing. Pearson's r falls too, but only from 0.161 to 0.137, and then levels off: shrinking scales the prediction down, which r does not see. That blindness is why R² chooses. Both curves score the inner splits; the 0.149 printed above is the refit, scored on the held-out folds.

    So the search lands on the grid's floor, and gridsearchCV warns, as it does whenever the choice is the smallest or the largest λ on offer: a curve still climbing at the edge would mean the search had been cut short. This one is not climbing. The grid starts two decades below the point where the curve stops changing, and extending it further would move the floor without moving the score. With 46 minutes at 250 Hz against ~1 450 design columns the normal equations are well conditioned, so the penalty is not what limits the fit, and the floor is the answer: in effect, the unpenalized least-squares solution.

    The held-out scores are highest over occipital sites, where visual responses to each new fixation are expected, and over frontal ones, where the potentials the eyes themselves generate at every saccade are largest. R² and r draw the same map, since on any one channel both grow with how much of it the kernels predict.

    5. The impulse kernels¶

    One column per feature: the butterfly, the channels × delay image and a topomap at the GFP peak. With a single subject there is no cluster test to shade.

    Amplitudes are in µV per event. The model was fitted on standardized columns, and its figures undo that, coef_ · σ_EEG / σ_x (kernel_units="original", the default); feature_units supplies the event in the label. coef_ itself stays in the standardized units it was fitted in.

    The kernels carry an arbitrary offset, so for display they are baseline-corrected over the pre-event part of the window. plot_baseline only affects figures; the stored kernels stay untouched.

    These are joint estimates. Each kernel is the response to its event over and above what the other predictors already explain: ontarget is what a target fixation adds to an ordinary one, and saccade is the response to a saccade of typical amplitude, since the amplitude effect lives in the spline block.

    6. The saccade response as a function of amplitude¶

    The sacc_amp block holds one kernel per spline column, and no single column means anything alone. What does mean something is their combination at a given amplitude a: the response to one saccade of that size is the saccade kernel plus each spline kernel weighted by that column's value at a.

    The figures above are already in µV per event, because they convert as they draw. This combination is built from coef_, which stays in standardized units, so here the conversion is done by hand: each kernel is divided by its column's standard deviation, giving a response per event, and multiplied by each channel's standard deviation, which returns µV. The result is an ERP-like response at any amplitude, in the units of the figures above and baseline-corrected like them.

    First, the basis itself over the amplitude distribution. The quantile knots put its resolution where most saccades are. The column missing from the partition of unity is the one drop="mean" removed, the one peaking nearest the mean amplitude:

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    grid = np.linspace(amplitudes.min(), amplitudes.max(), 300)
columns = sacc_amp_basis.transform(grid[:, None])

ax.hist(amplitudes, bins=60, color="0.85", density=True)
ax.set(xlabel="saccade amplitude (deg)", ylabel="density", yticks=[])
basis_ax = ax.twinx()
basis_ax.plot(grid, columns, lw=2)
basis_ax.set(ylabel="basis value", ylim=(0, 1.05))
ax.set_title(f"{N_SPLINES} spline columns over the amplitude distribution")
fig.tight_layout()

    The standard deviations are the ones the figures convert with, over every non-rejected sample. The model does not expose them, so they are recomputed here.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    # Scales the kernels were fitted in, over the non-rejected samples.
eeg_sd = np.nanstd(raw.get_data(reject_by_annotation="nan"), axis=1)
onset_sd = features["saccade"][good, 0].std()
spline_sd = sacc_amp_basis.transform(features["sacc_amp"][good]).std(axis=0)

onset_kernel = model.coef_["saccade"].cpu().numpy()[:, 0] / onset_sd            # (ch, delays)
spline_kernels = model.coef_["sacc_amp"].cpu().numpy() / spline_sd[:, None]     # (ch, k, delays)


def saccade_response(amplitude_deg) -> np.ndarray:
    """µV response to one saccade of each amplitude: (n_amplitudes, channels, delays)."""
    weights = sacc_amp_basis.transform(np.asarray(amplitude_deg, dtype=float)[:, None])
    per_event = onset_kernel[None] + np.einsum("ak,ckd->acd", weights, spline_kernels)
    microvolts = per_event * eeg_sd[None, :, None] * 1e6
    return microvolts - microvolts[..., baseline].mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)


lag_min = int(round(SACCADE_WINDOW[0] * SAMPLE_RATE))
times_ms = (lag_min + np.arange(onset_kernel.shape[-1])) / SAMPLE_RATE * 1e3
baseline = times_ms <= 0          # PLOT_BASELINE, as a delay mask
    # Scales the kernels were fitted in, over the non-rejected samples. eeg_sd = np.nanstd(raw.get_data(reject_by_annotation="nan"), axis=1) onset_sd = features["saccade"][good, 0].std() spline_sd = sacc_amp_basis.transform(features["sacc_amp"][good]).std(axis=0) onset_kernel = model.coef_["saccade"].cpu().numpy()[:, 0] / onset_sd # (ch, delays) spline_kernels = model.coef_["sacc_amp"].cpu().numpy() / spline_sd[:, None] # (ch, k, delays) def saccade_response(amplitude_deg) -> np.ndarray: """µV response to one saccade of each amplitude: (n_amplitudes, channels, delays).""" weights = sacc_amp_basis.transform(np.asarray(amplitude_deg, dtype=float)[:, None]) per_event = onset_kernel[None] + np.einsum("ak,ckd->acd", weights, spline_kernels) microvolts = per_event * eeg_sd[None, :, None] * 1e6 return microvolts - microvolts[..., baseline].mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True) lag_min = int(round(SACCADE_WINDOW[0] * SAMPLE_RATE)) times_ms = (lag_min + np.arange(onset_kernel.shape[-1])) / SAMPLE_RATE * 1e3 baseline = times_ms <= 0 # PLOT_BASELINE, as a delay mask

    Five amplitudes, from the 10th to the 90th percentile of the distribution. The channel to follow is read off the data rather than chosen by hand: the one largest in magnitude at the peak of the global field power of the median-amplitude response, within 0–300 ms.

    The peak is then read separately at every amplitude, because amplitude changes both how large the response is and when it peaks. A larger saccade lasts longer, so the fixation it ends starts later. Reading every amplitude at one fixed latency would confuse the two effects.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    AMPLITUDES = np.round(np.percentile(amplitudes, [10, 30, 50, 70, 90]), 1)
responses = saccade_response(AMPLITUDES)

median_response = saccade_response([np.median(amplitudes)])[0]
search = (times_ms >= 0) & (times_ms <= 300)
gfp_peak = np.flatnonzero(search)[median_response[:, search].std(axis=0).argmax()]
channel = np.abs(median_response[:, gfp_peak]).argmax()
sign = np.sign(median_response[channel, gfp_peak])
print(f"GFP peak at {times_ms[gfp_peak]:.0f} ms -> channel {raw.ch_names[channel]}")


def peaks(response):
    # Index and value of the largest deflection of that sign within 0-300 ms.
    index = np.flatnonzero(search)[(sign * response[..., search]).argmax(axis=-1)]
    return index, np.take_along_axis(response, index[..., None], axis=-1)[..., 0]


# Curves stop at the 95th percentile, past which there are too few saccades to trust.
curve_grid = grid[grid <= np.percentile(amplitudes, 95)]
grid_index, grid_value = peaks(saccade_response(curve_grid)[:, channel])
amp_index, amp_value = peaks(responses[:, channel])

colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0, 0.9, len(AMPLITUDES)))
fig, (wave_ax, size_ax, time_ax) = plt.subplots(
    1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.8), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.6, 1, 1]))
for amplitude, response, color in zip(AMPLITUDES, responses, colors):
    wave_ax.plot(times_ms, response[channel], color=color, lw=2, label=f"{amplitude:g}°")
wave_ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
wave_ax.axvline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
wave_ax.set(xlabel="delay from saccade onset (ms)", ylabel="µV per saccade",
            title=f"{raw.ch_names[channel]}: response by saccade amplitude")
wave_ax.legend(title="amplitude", fontsize=8, frameon=False)

for ax, values, label, points in [
        (size_ax, grid_value, "peak (µV per saccade)", amp_value),
        (time_ax, times_ms[grid_index], "peak latency (ms)", times_ms[amp_index])]:
    ax.plot(curve_grid, values, color="k", lw=2)
    ax.scatter(AMPLITUDES, points, c=colors, zorder=3, s=40)
    shown = amplitudes[amplitudes <= curve_grid.max()]
    ax.plot(shown, np.full_like(shown, values.min()), "|",
            color="0.6", ms=8, alpha=0.2)
    ax.set(xlabel="saccade amplitude (deg)", ylabel=label)
for ax in (wave_ax, size_ax, time_ax):
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout()
